It’s five answers to five questions. Here we go…
h
1. A coworker asked me whether he should report my boss for screaming
q

My boss, Robert, has a reputation for speaking loudly (to the verge of screaming) and being very blunt and direct. However, he’s well-liked by many people: he’s a hard worker and a fair boss. New people have heard “If he screams, don’t worry, it’s just how he speaks,” and after years of knowing him, I’ve found it to be mostly true.
q

Today, my coworker Mark (whose boss is not Robert) asked to speak with me in private. He told me he was present when his own employee, Zach, was heavily screamed at and borderline insulted by Robert. He insisted that, while everyone is accustomed to Robert’s way of speaking, he thinks this crossed the line this time. Moreover, Zach was deeply affected by the altercation, felt physically unwell after it, and confided in Mark about how he was feeling. Mark feels Zach expects him to do something.
q

Mark asked me if he should talk to the department director (Robert’s boss). I suggested speaking first with his own boss, but his boss is a very close friend of Robert. He also said he doesn’t trust HR, since Robert is high in the chain of command and he fears a complaint against him wouldn’t be handled impartially. I felt deeply uncomfortable because Robert is my own boss. I actually like Robert (which doesn’t excuse the behavior at all) and while I wasn’t present in this altercation, I have no reason to doubt Mark. How could I have reacted? Is there any alternative I could suggest to Mark? Should I say anything to Robert at all?
p

It sounds like your office has grown way too comfortable with a grown man screaming at people. That’s not in any way okay! It may be “just how he speaks,” but then how he speaks is abusive. And now with Zach, it’s apparently not just screaming but being “borderline insulting”? This is all a really big deal!
p

This isn’t something you should normalize or excuse away, and I think it’s worth considering that your norms have gotten warped by working around it for a while. Zach is very normal in feeling deeply affected and physically unwell after being screamed at and insulted, and Mark is right to want to escalate it to Robert’s boss.
p

As for how you could have responded to Mark, one option is to support him in taking this to someone with some power over Robert. There’s nothing here for you to take back to Robert; that puts you in a position of trying to referee your own boss, and you don’t have the positional authority to do that. Instead, let Mark know you recognize that Robert’s behavior has become too normalized and that he and Zach have every right to take issue with it.
p

2. Do I have to invite my coworker to my family Thanksgiving?
q

A coworker found out I was hosting Thanksgiving and pretty openly hinted that they had nowhere to go. Am I obligated to invite them to my family celebration? I work pretty frequently with this person and they’re nice enough (as in, I wouldn’t mind grabbing coffee or something with them occasionally), but I don’t want to mix my family world and my work world. But now I feel guilty — they seemed really gloomy about not having anywhere to go this year.
p
It would be a kind thing to invite them if you wanted to, but you don’t want to, and it’s reasonable to prefer not to mix work and family in that way.
p

For many families, Thanksgiving isn’t just a casual social gathering; it’s often a deeply family-steeped occasion, with traditions, relationships, and a specific atmosphere that family members like to preserve (or that you might rather not expose a coworker to!). Some families do very much have a “the more the merrier” vibe at their Thanksgivings, but it’s okay if yours isn’t one of them. Feeling compassion for your coworker’s situation doesn’t mean you’re responsible for solving it on this specific day.
h
3. Can my wife ask her boss to stop sending gifts I’m allergic to?
q

This is likely the world’s lowest-stakes question, but I thought I’d ask anyway. Every year for the holidays, my wife’s skip level boss sends a very nice box of VERY nice baked goods that come uncooked so you can make fresh and delicious cookies, cinnamon rolls, and other delicious treats. The problem is, I have celiac disease and we keep a gluten free kitchen, so this very nice gift almost always becomes trash unless I can find someone to take it before it goes bad.
q

We just received this year’s box for the fourth year, and my question is would it be complely out of line for my wife to ask for something different because of her spouse’s allergy? Should I just let this go and take it in the spirit it is offered? (I should just let it go, shouldn’t I?) I just hate to see so much waste, and I truly wish we could enjoy this otherwise nice gift.
p

It’s too late for this year since it’s already arrived, but next year around late September/early October, she could mention it to him — framing it as, “In past years you’ve very kindly sent those lovely boxes of baked goods. We’re not able to keep them because my spouse has celiac disease and we can’t have gluten in the house, so I wanted to let you know before you spend money on one for us this year. But I really appreciate the thought and appreciate you thinking of us!!”
p
The right move would be for her boss’s boss to then send her a different item. I can’t guarantee that they will, but a gracious gift-giver would.
h
4. How can I convince HR to let me work a second job?
q

I took a job four years ago with the dangling carrot of advancement at the two- or three-year mark. That hasn’t materialized, and now I find myself struggling with the salary that hasn’t kept up with inflation. I have been told in no uncertain terms that salary negotiation is not an available option, and I can take the annual 3% raise or I can leave.
q
What are some of the things I should consider when having a conversation with HR about taking on a second job?
q

I vaguely remember reading in an employee handbook that I would need to get approval for this and that I can’t get a role that would be seen as competition with my current job. My goal is something that would primarily be nights and weekends.
q

I don’t want the conversation with HR to sound like I’m whining or complaining, but it is critical that I do something and I don’t want it to result in me losing my job. How do I explain this in a pragmatic way and get them to say yes so I can keep taking care of my family?
p

First, make sure you actually do need their approval. Relying on a vague recollection isn’t enough; get out the handbook and see exactly what it says, because you may not even need to alert them at all (or may only need their permission for certain types of work or in certain circumstances).
p

But if you do, then be matter-of-fact: “I’m planning on applying for a part-time job doing X and I saw in the handbook that I’d need approval for that. What do you need from me for that process?” In other words, keep it logistics-focused. I think you’re picturing that you’ll need to convince them, and it’s far more likely to just be a bureaucratic process where they want to make sure the other job won’t pose a conflict of interest, and it’ll be a straightforward yes or no, not a “convince us we should say yes.”
h
5. How much notice should I give when I retire?
q

I will be retiring next year (a couple of years ahead of the norm for my location and age bracket) so I’m preparing to give notice. I’m leaving on very good terms — I love my job, my boss is wonderful, the company is very successful. The only reason I’m leaving is indeed because I’m in a position to retire early! My boss knows I am likely to retire early but we haven’t talked specific timing yet.
q

In my role, the standard is four weeks notice, but I’m happy to give longer. I’m thinking three months. My thoughts are: resign to my boss a week before they go on their annual three-week break; that gives me four weeks to spread the word and start seeking expressions of interest to take my role (I’m hoping for an internal candidate); once the boss is back, the interviews are done and a successful candidate appointed; that person then needs to give four weeks notice of their own role; then I do two or three weeks handover before my departure.
q

I’m aware that they may say “thanks but no thanks — you can leave in a month,” but I am pretty confident that won’t happen. I just wanted to get a sanity check on whether my outline makes sense or is too generous or presents any risks I haven’t thought of?
p

The risks of long notice periods are (a) you’ll be told to leave earlier than you wanted to go, (b) you’ll start getting left out of projects earlier than you anticipated (which makes sense since work is being transitioned) and you’ll be bored / feel like your time isn’t being well used, or (c) the transition will still wait for the last minute and you’ll end up annoyed that you offered so much time.
p

It doesn’t sound like the first one is a concern, and the other two are more annoyances than serious problems. If I were going to nitpick your plan, I’d just say that four weeks is a lot longer than it will really take to spread the word … and also your proposed timeline assumes a very orderly transition, but in a lot of jobs it wouldn’t happen that way; other things would get in the way, interviews would be pushed back, the hiring process will get drawn out longer, etc. But it’s still a reasonable amount of notice to give if you want to, and it’s pretty normal to give more notice when you’re retiring than when you’re just moving to another job, so if this is the plan that feels best to you, it’s perfectly fine to do it this way.
